To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the overall evidence is inconclusive, 2) the evidence on dietary fat and meat is weak, 3) the evidence for fibre, fruit and vegetable is inconclusive, and 4) the evidence on low physical activity and obesity is strong.
about 1.5% of all cancer cases in Nordic women around the year 2 000 are attributable to low physical activity, 1.5-2.0% to obesity and about 1% to a low intake of fruit and vegetables.
the following cancer cases can be predicted in 2000 in the Nordic countries: (i) 625 cancer cases in men and women caused by obesity, and (ii) 1.5% of all cancers caused by low physical activity.

the role of diet in carcinogenesis, with special emphasis on dietary factors that may influence the development and growth of cancer.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
diet is an important risk factor for cancer.
the evidence is insufficient to estimate the numbers and proportion of cancers that could have been avoided by a better diet and by a healthy body weight.
the evidence is not yet sufficient to make any reliable estimate of the numbers and percentages of cancers that could have been avoided through well-defined dietary and physical-activity habits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the number of avoidable cancers due to low physical activity and obesity could be estimated to 625 around the year 2010 in the Nordic countries, and the proportion of avoidable cancers would be around 1% in women and less than1% in men.
the numbers of avoidable cancer cases in the Nordic countries are small.

the Nordic countries could avoid about 1% (1,500 cases) of the total number of cancer cases around the year 2015 through a combination of a healthy diet, regular physical activity and a healthy body weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk for avoidable cancers in the population could be reduced if we could increase our physical activity and maintain a healthy body weight.
the Nordic countries have made substantial progress during recent decades in reducing the risk of cancer through improved public health.
the evidence is not yet conclusive on the role of dietary and lifestyle factors on the risk of cancer, and that the numbers of cancers that can be avoided by changes in lifestyle are small.
